newsitem.title: INDIA: India gears up to end state broadcast monopoly.
newsitem.headline: India gears up to end state broadcast monopoly.

text.p: The Indian cabinet decided on Monday to set up a committee to prepare the ground for a bill which could end a state monopoly over radio and television and allow private broadcasters, a government spokesman said.

"The government has decided to constitute a sub-committee to study the various constitutional and legal implications of the broadcast bill, and the committee should complete its work in a fortnight, so that the government should introduce the bill during the budget session (of parliament)," he told Reuters.
The budget session, set to begin in the second half of February, usually runs until May. The proposed bill must be passed by the upper and lower houses of parliament to take effect as law.
The spokesman did not give details on who the members of the government sub-committee would be.
India began opening up key sectors under an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991.

But the state still owns radio and television stations which broadcast from India, and there has been strong opposition to opening up broadcast media to the private sector, particularly foreign broadcasters.
Information and Broadcasting Minister C.M. Ibrahim was quoted last year as saying the government would not allow foreign broadcasting networks to enter India.
The spokesman said on Monday the broadcast bill was expected to cover cable television, the regulation of airwaves and the licensing of private broadcasters in future.
It would also cover Prasar Bharati, a proposed autonomous state-funded broadcasting authority on the lines of the British Broadcasting Corporation, he added.
"The government is for the first time framing a comprehensive broadcast law as well as a Prasar Bharati Bill," he said.
The government leases out time-slots to private producers, but news programmes are subject to restrictions.

Dozens of time-slots are available to private producers with stipulated proportions of advertising time, but they cannot set up their own stations to air their programmes or acquire broadcast frequencies.
Things began to change five years ago when Hong Kong-based cable broadcaster Star Television, later taken over by media baron Rupert Murdoch's New Corp, began beaming into the country.

Other private broadcasters in Hindi and regional Indian languages soon started beaming into India from locations as far away as Russia and the Philippines, and gradually built up a strong lobby to free up the airwaves.
The growth of cable television gave the Indian audience a wider choice and whetted its appetite for private broadcasts.
The government was pushed towards permitting private broadcasts in 1995, when the Supreme Court said that airwaves were a public property and the state did not have a monopoly.
Earlier the government had reluctantly set up an autonomous broadcasting authority after opposition critics claimed state media had been used for political propaganda.
